newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FEATURE-Sampan Annie hedges bets on life with Beijing.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Sampan Annie hedges bets on life with Beijing.

text.p: Flashing a gold- toothed smile, tough navigator Annie takes tourists on harbour trips in her traditional sampan craft. And she's hedging bets about her future when China takes over Hong Kong from Britain.
She sells souvenirs from an ancient brassbound box on the deck of her little, banana-shaped wooden boat, bobbing like a small junk over sunlit Aberdeen harbour.

Here, for a few dollars, is something for lots of political fates. To mark the present twilight era of British rule ending on June 30, there are lurid T-shirts with emblems like: "I survived Hong Kong."

For the immediate future there's an item still rarely seen here, red-starred, army-style green caps from the mainland. No one in Hong Kong wears this symbol of communism, only to be found in a few curio shops for sale to foreigners.
TURNING POINT IN HISTORY FOR HONG KONG
And for devotees of retro-chic, she offers long-abandoned symbols of Chinese humiliation under the old, alien Manchu dynasty -- pill-box hats with pigtails that millions once wore.
"What do you think -- good?" she laughs. "Very cheap, yes?"
Annie -- all that she will reveal of her identity -- is seemingly uncommitted at a turning point in history for Hong Kong's six and a half million people, 98 percent of them Chinese.

She is from the indigenous Tanka population on Hong Kong island's south coast, a secretive clan of former pirates and now fishing craft-owners. They live on picturesque boats in Aberdeen, known to the Chinese as "Little Hong Kong".
Wearing giant straw hats and floral-patterned grey pyjamas, she and a few other women run the harbour sightseeing business -- a trade apparently reserved for them by custom.

They usually work in pairs. A partner on shore rustles up business by negotiating a price with passing tourists on the promenade. She then signals the approach of customers with a raised umbrella, visible to the boatwoman below.
FLOATING RESTAURANTS, COLONIAL GRAVE SITES
An hour-long trip on boats like Annie's sampan is one of Hong Kong's tourist delights. The motor-driven little junk has open sides for fresh air and viewing and a curved canvas top supported by rods.

It weaves past the famous "jumbo" floating restaurants and among huge houseboats whose rooftops are crammed with thousands of netted fish drying in the sun, finally passing hillside graves of forgotten colonial-era worthies.
There are in fact two separate cemeteries, one for the British and another for the Chinese. Even in death, the 19th century ruling power insisted on racial segregation.
Fraternisation, residential areas, and government jobs were denied to Chinese for much of the last century.
Open displays of racial prejudice against Asians were common up to World War Two when conquering Japanese forces inflicted a humiliating defeat on the imperial power.
It was the first nail in the coffin of colonialism that will be completed when Britain hands Hong Kong back to China.
PRAYING FOR PEACE, PROSPERITY

The cemeteries overlook an historically vulnerable area, including the nearby, once-fortified Stanley harbour where the 19th century Britons feared a sneak naval attack by potential foes Russia or France.
Annie rolls her eyes and makes a throat-slitting gesture with her hand as she navigates past the cemeteries. "No good, huh?", an apparent comment on mortality.
Reaching shore, Annie has a final prudent thought. She removes the red star from a cap purchased by a Western visitor and hands it over separately. "May be better -- what think?"
Half a dozen customers -- a boatload -- are waiting for her next trip. Annie helps them aboard and points to a temple a few hundred yards (metres) away.
In the dimly-lit, oven-hot interior, her clanswomen are lighting joss sticks before an altar to the Goddess of the Sea, known here as Tin Hau. "Peace and prosperity," they murmur in prayer.
